Empirical Research Plan – “Women’s Political Representation and Public-Goods Provision in Indian Village Councils”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Strategy: Random-assignment (experimental) design implemented through India’s mandatory lottery.  
Implementation: Estimate intent-to-treat (ITT) effects by comparing reserved and unreserved GPs in the first election cycle after the 73rd Amendment came into force.  Because assignment is by lottery, a simple difference in means (or OLS with controls) delivers unbiased causal estimates.  To improve precision and handle any small, chance imbalances we include district fixed effects and pre-treatment covariates.  
Optional extensions:  
• Instrument actual female head (=1 if elected head is a woman) with reservation status (two-stage least squares) to obtain the local average treatment effect (LATE) when non-compliance occurs.  
• If data cover ≥2 election cycles, add GP fixed effects and estimate a two-period difference-in-differences to soak up persistent GP heterogeneity.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable: RESERVE_gp = 1 if the GP head seat was randomly reserved for a woman in the focal election, 0 otherwise.  
Control group: All GPs that were not reserved for a woman in that same election.  
Timing: Use outcomes measured during the full five-year term of that elected council (e.g., 1999–2004 for West Bengal, 2000–2005 for Rajasthan).  Pre-treatment outcomes (before the amendment or before the first post-amendment election) will be used for balance checks and placebo tests.  
(No running variable or cutoff is required; this is not an RDD.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Randomization: The state governments implement a true lottery and do not manipulate the draw.  
Plausibility: Public lotteries were conducted in open meetings; contemporaneous press reports confirm transparency.

A2. Stable Unit Treatment Value (SUTVA): Public-goods outcomes in one GP are unaffected by the reservation status of neighboring GPs.  
Plausibility: Most GP budgets are internally generated plus formula-based transfers; spillovers likely modest, though inter-village roads could create some externalities.

A3. No differential measurement error: Data quality is independent of reservation status.  
Plausibility: Survey enumerators were blind to the paper’s hypotheses; however, subjective condition ratings may still be colored by respondents’ expectations.

A4. Full coverage: All randomly assigned GPs are observed in the data set (no attrition correlated with treatment).  
Plausibility: The census of GPs in sampled districts was covered; any attrition would come from survey non-response at the household level, which we can test.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Mitigation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Threat 1: Non-compliance – a woman is the formal head but her husband or a male relative is de-facto leader (“proxy female”).  
Mitigation:  
• Estimate reduced-form ITT (robust to non-compliance).  
• Collect leader background data (education, decision autonomy) and control/explore heterogeneity.  
• Instrument actual female decision-maker with reservation to get LATE.

Threat 2: Spillovers – neighboring unreserved GPs may benefit from roads or water projects initiated by a reserved GP.  
Mitigation:  
• Include district fixed effects; cluster standard errors at the block (sub-district) or higher level.  
• Sensitivity analysis excluding GPs sharing long borders with treated GPs.  
• Spatial lag model as robustness.

Threat 3: Chance imbalance in covariates because the sample is not the full universe (265 + 100 GPs).  
Mitigation:  
• Present balance table; if covariates differ at p<.10, include them as controls.  
• Re-weight by inverse probability of selection if sampling probabilities differ across treatment status.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages -------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast data handling
library(fixest)       # high-performance fixed-effect estimation
library(AER)          # ivreg for 2SLS
library(sandwich)     # robust vcov
library(modelsummary) # neat tables

# 1. Data Loading ---------------------------------------------------
dt  <- fread("gp_public_goods.csv")        # GP-level outcomes
hh  <- fread("household_survey.csv")       # household preferences / complaints
lead<- fread("leader_characteristics.csv") # demographics of heads

# 2. Merge and Variable Construction --------------------------------
dt <- merge(dt, lead, by = "gp_id", all.x = TRUE)
dt[, reserve  := as.integer(reserved == 1)]           # 1 = reserved seat
dt[, female_hd:= as.integer(head_gender == "F")]      # actual gender
# Outcomes (examples)
dt[, water_fac := drinking_water_no]                  # number of water points
dt[, road_cond := road_cond_index]                    # higher = better roads
dt[, irrig_fac := irrigation_no]
dt[, edu_fac   := school_buildings]

# Control set
ctr_vars <- c("population", "sc_st_share", "literacy_rate", "poverty_rate")

# 3. Main ITT Regression -------------------------------------------
# Example for drinking water
itt <- feols(water_fac ~ reserve + state + district | 0,
             data = dt, cluster = ~district)
etable(itt, se = "cluster")

# 4. IV Regression (LATE) ------------------------------------------
iv <- feols(water_fac ~ 1 | reserve ~ female_hd,
            data = dt, cluster = ~district)
etable(itt, iv, se = "cluster", keep = c("reserve","female_hd"))

# 5. Robustness Check: Placebo (pre-period outcome) -----------------
# Assume pre_water_fac is number of water points before reservation
placebo <- feols(pre_water_fac ~ reserve + state + district | 0,
                 data = dt, cluster = ~district)
etable(placebo, se = "cluster")

# 6. Robustness Check: Covariate-adjusted ---------------------------
itt_adj <- feols(water_fac ~ reserve + state + district + population +
                 sc_st_share + literacy_rate + poverty_rate,
                 data = dt, cluster = ~district)
etable(itt, itt_adj, se = "cluster")
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Theory and qualitative evidence suggest women place higher weight on time-saving infrastructure (clean drinking water close to home, all-weather roads).  I expect:  
• +10–15 % increase in the number of drinking-water facilities;  
• +0.2–0.3 standard-deviation improvement in a road-quality index;  
• No statistically significant change (or even slight reductions) in irrigation facilities and new school buildings.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (Randomized Design)
(1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable/absent)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Successful random assignment verified by balance tests ………………… 1  
C2: Low differential attrition / full coverage ……………………………………… 0.5 (survey non-response possible)  
C3: SUTVA – minimal interference across GPs ………………………………… 0.5  
C4: No spillover or contamination in implementation ……………………… 0.5  
C5: High compliance with assignment (female head in reserved seat) … 0.5  

Total = 3 / 5.  Most assumptions look reasonable but spillovers and proxy-female issues require careful robustness analyses.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
This plan delivers transparent, policy-relevant causal estimates of how mandated female representation alters local public-goods provision in rural India.
